en.title: Fairest Lord Jesus
en.author: Anonymous German, Münster Gesangbuch, 1677
en.translator: Richard Storrs Willis (sts. 1-3, 1850); Joseph A. Seiss (st. 4, 1873)
stanzas:
[D]Fairest Lord Jesus, [G]Ruler of all [A]nature,
O [D]Thou of God and [A7]man the [D]Son,
[D]Thee will I cherish, [G]Thee will I [A]honor,
[D]Thou, my soul's [G]glory, [A7]joy and [D]crown.

Fair are the meadows, fairer still the woodlands,
Robed in the blooming garb of spring;
Jesus is fairer, Jesus is purer,
Who makes the woeful heart to sing.

Fair is the sunshine, fairer still the moonlight,
And all the twinkling starry host;
Jesus shines brighter, Jesus shines purer
Than all the angels heav'n can boast.

Beautiful Savior! Lord of all the nations!
Son of God and Son of Man!
Glory and honor, praise, adoration,
Now and forevermore be Thine.

notes: The four commonly-printed stanzas, in the Timeless Truths wording (traditional capitalisation). ONE STANZA DELIBERATELY OMITTED: Timeless Truths prints a fifth, "All fairest beauty, heavenly and earthly", and credits it to Lilian Stevenson (1870-1960). That is a 20th-century translation whose public-domain status I could not establish, so it is left out; hymnary's representative text (United Methodist Hymnal 1989) likewise prints only these four. Attribution is genuinely tangled: the worklist names Richard S. Willis as translator, but hymnary says the translator of sts. 1-3 is anonymous and that the text first appeared in Willis's Church Chorals and Choir Studies (1850) — Willis may only have been the editor/arranger. Stanza 4 is Joseph A. Seiss's (1873). Underlying German is "Schönster Herr Jesu", Münster Gesangbuch 1677. Tune also known as ST. ELIZABETH / SCHÖNSTER HERR JESU (Silesian folk melody). Key D is hymnary's tune-page key, so the chart is at printed pitch; the Timeless Truths score is in F. (Re-verified 2026-08-01: hymnary's CRUSADERS' HYMN page does give D major and 5.6.8.5.5.8, so both the key and the meter recorded here are at source.) Text independently cross-checked against adventisthymns.com, which prints exactly these four stanzas with this wording; it reads "Thou art my glory, joy, and crown" in stanza 1 where this source has "Thou, my soul's glory, joy and crown" — "my soul's glory" is the far commoner reading and is kept. Wikipedia independently supports the attribution note above: it credits the "Beautiful Savior" stanza to Seiss (1873) and says Willis only ARRANGED the hymn for Church Chorals and Choir Studies (1850), which is why the worklist's bare "translator: Richard S. Willis" is not reproduced verbatim here. Wikipedia gives the meter as 8.8.4.4.8.8 with refrain; FORMAT.md says to record the meter as hymnary lists it, so 5.6.8.5.5.8 stands.
